issues.item: Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
issues.explanation: 'Being in nature similar to where it happened' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of life-threatening illness, which typically involves medical/health contexts rather than a natural-environment trauma setting.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: 'Avoid grief reminders' implies bereavement/loss of another person, which does not fit the stated trauma type of life-threatening illness unless there is an unreported death-related trauma; it is not supported by the other selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: 'Fear of rage' is weakly connected to the rest of the profile: the other appraisals and memory items center on damage, unreality, and role failure after illness, not anger-based dyscontrol. This makes the appraisal set less internally coherent.

vignette: The crisis began on a Tuesday in late autumn when Mei Ling collapsed at her kitchen counter, a sudden infection sending her body into rapid shock. Rushed to the trauma center, the emergency department's sharp antiseptic scent and the relentless draft of the cooling system became the first anchors of what followed. For hours, the medical narrative blurred into fragments: a nurse's urgent voice, the cold bite of an IV line sliding into her arm, the rhythmic hiss of a ventilator mask. Some moments remained razor-sharp-the exact temperature of the chilled saline, the glint of a steel needle connecting to the tubing-while other stretches of the week slipped into absolute white silence. She had come to believe that the story of what happened was too extreme to be real, as if it belonged to someone else, yet her body had learned to react as though it were still happening. When a cold draft brushed her neck, or when she caught the faint medicinal odor of a colleague's hand sanitizer in the office, her pulse would spike without warning. She was certain that her body had been permanently damaged by the illness, leaving her to assume she could no longer trust her own physical limits. Over the following months, Mei found herself navigating between opposing efforts to manage the intrusion. She tried to erase the memory of the event, deliberately turning away from health magazines and muting any news segment that mentioned epidemics. Simultaneously, she had come to believe that she was slowly losing her grip on reality, so she began constantly monitoring her own thoughts for any sign of going crazy, tallying every intrusive sensation as proof that her mind was fracturing. The fear that her life had been destroyed by the illness settled heavily on her shoulders, particularly because she felt she had failed in her most important role as a mother and partner. Her husband noticed how she flinched when he mentioned a routine physician visit, and how she avoided looking at medical equipment altogether. She stopped going to hospitals, declined emergency services, and sidestepped physical examinations. What frightened her most was that the illness had arrived without warning, leaving her to assume that any unexplained ache could be the beginning of another collapse. This pattern intersected directly with her work as a project manager overseeing a commercial development. When the company's occupational health clinic scheduled mandatory post-illness clearance screenings, Mei found herself unable to walk through the clinic doors. The thought of needles, drips, and sterile air made her breath shorten, so she began emailing her supervisors that she required a medical exemption. The office HVAC system blew cold air directly across her workstation, and she spent hours drafting emails to HR requesting a workspace near the radiators, though she told no one why. The avoidance slowly bled into her professional obligations; she delegated two major site inspections, missed a crucial zoning meeting, and watched her reputation for reliability fracture. At home, the winter cold deepened her isolation, and she kept her thermostat high to ward off the temperature that triggered her panic. Her husband's quiet concern turned into distance when she stopped discussing future plans, convinced that her physical vulnerability meant she had nothing left to offer her family. Today, at forty-two, Mei sat for an intake appointment after a sudden wave of grief and terror hit her during a team dinner. There was no image, no specific memory, only the full emotional intensity of the event crashing over her while she sat quietly at the table. Her husband had gently suggested she speak with someone who understood how the body and mind respond to near-death illness. She is most afraid that without intervention, the fear will continue to dictate her schedule and relationships, but she is hoping that someone might help her reconcile the fragments of what happened with the reality of waking up each morning. She wants to stop watching her life shrink into avoidance, and to believe that her body can still be trusted.
